en: Biographies of Divine Monks, Volume One: Kāśyapa Mātanga.
Kāśyapa Mātanga was originally a native of Central India. He possessed a refined and elegant bearing and was learned in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
He constantly took traveling and teaching as his primary vocation.
While he was lecturing on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in a small tributary state of India,
an enemy nation invaded the borders.
Teng reflected, saying:
"The Sūtra states that those who can expound this Dharma are protected by the earth deities."
It was intended to make those who dwell there peaceful and happy;
yet now that the clash of spears and arrows has only just begun,
how could this possibly be beneficial?
He then vowed to forget his own person and went in person to mediate and persuade,
ultimately bringing about friendly relations between the two nations.
Because of this, his reputation was widely proclaimed.
During the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, Emperor Ming dreamed at night of a golden man flying through the air and arriving.
He then assembled his high ministers to interpret the dream.
Fu Yi, a man of broad learning, submitted a memorial,
saying: "Your servant has heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions whose name is Buddha."
"Is that which Your Majesty dreamed not surely this?
The Emperor agreed with this,
and immediately dispatched Langzhong Cai Yin, the disciple of the Doctor Qin Jing, and others.
They traveled to India in search of the Buddha-dharma.
There, Kang Sengcai and his companions encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga,
who invited them to return to the land of Han.
Teng vowed to propagate the teachings and did not shrink from exhaustion or hardship;
braving the shifting sands, he reached Luoyang.
Emperor Ming received him with great honor and hospitality.
A vihāra was established outside the western gate of the city to house him;
thus, the presence of śramaṇas in the land of Han began with Dharmaratna.
However, as the Great Dharma had only recently been transmitted and there were yet no believers,
he kept his profound understanding within himself and did not proclaim it.
He eventually passed away in Luoyang.
A record states:
Anzheng translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* in one fascicle;
it was initially sealed away in the fourteenth chamber of the Stone Chamber at the Lan Tai.
The place where [An Shigao] resided is the Baima Monastery outside the Yong Gate to the west of present-day Luoyang.
According to tradition:
In a foreign land there was once a king who destroyed various monasteries;
however, he had not yet reached the Jātīśvara Monastery.
At night, a white horse circled the stupa and neighed piteously.
He immediately informed the King,
who thereupon halted the destruction of the various monasteries;
consequently, he changed the name of Zhaoti to Baima.
Therefore, when naming various monasteries,
many took this as their standard.
[The names] Falan and Zhufa Lan [are derived from this].
He was a native of Central India.
He claimed to have recited tens of thousands of chapters of sutras and treatises,
serving as a teacher to the scholars of India.
At that time, when Cai Yin had arrived in that country,
Kāla and Mātanga had already entered into an agreement to travel together for the purpose of conversion;
they subsequently followed him back.
Having arrived in Luoyang, he stayed with Fotiao for a short while and soon became proficient in the Chinese language.
Zhi Cien had obtained scriptures from the Western Regions.
He immediately translated them;
namely, five works including the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga*, the *Buddhajanma-saṃgraha*, the *Buddhacarita-samudra-kośa*, the *Buddhacarita*, and the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.
Later, due to the relocation of the capital and the turmoil of invasions, four of these works lost their original manuscripts and were no longer transmitted.
In the region east of the Yangtze River, only the Sutra in Forty-two Sections remains extant today;
it consists of approximately two thousand words.
Among all the sūtras currently extant in the land of Han, this is the very first.
An Shigao also obtained from the Western Regions a painted image of Śākyamuni in a reclining posture;
it was the fourth work produced by the master who fashioned the sandalwood image for King Udayana.
Upon arriving in Luoyang,
Emperor Ming immediately ordered artists to paint copies of them, which were placed within the Qingliang Terrace and atop Mount Xianjie Ling;
the original images no longer exist today.
Furthermore, in the past, when Emperor Wu of Han dredged the bottom of Kunming Lake and found black ash, he questioned Dongfang Shuo.
Shuo said, "You may ask the Brahmans from the Western Regions."
When Dharmaratna arrived,
the assembly questioned him,
to which he replied:
"When the world reaches its end and the kalpa-fire burns through everything,
these ashes shall remain.
These words are indeed proven by this evidence.
Those who believed in him were very numerous.
Later, he passed away in Luoyang at the age of over sixty.
An Shigao, whose courtesy name was An Qing,
was the prince of the kingdom of Parthia (Anxi).
From his youth, he was renowned for his filial conduct.
Furthermore, his aspirations were resolute and his intellect sharp; he applied himself with diligence to learning.
He attained a thorough mastery of foreign classics, the seven luminaries and the five elements, medical prescriptions, and diverse arts, even down to the cries of birds and beasts.
Once, while traveling,
he suddenly saw a flock of swallows and said to his companions:
"The swallows say."
"There ought to be someone to deliver food.
Shortly thereafter, food was indeed brought there.
The assembly all marveled at this.
His outstanding reputation had already spread to the Western Regions early on.
He abdicated his kingdom to leave the household life and cultivate the Way;
he was extensively learned in the Piṭaka, being especially proficient in the study of Abhidharma.
Subsequently, he traveled abroad, visiting various countries,
and arrived in China at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty.
There, he became proficient in the Chinese language and translated numerous sutras.
There were many miraculous signs.
He claimed that in a previous life he had already left the household life.
He had a fellow student who was prone to great anger.
Whenever he went on his alms-round and encountered donors whose offerings were not to his liking, he would invariably express resentment and harbor grudges;
Hui-gao repeatedly admonished and exhorted him.
He never reformed his ways.
After more than twenty years had passed in this manner,
he took leave of his fellow students, saying:
"I shall go to fully exhaust the karmic retributions from our past lives.
Although you are learned in the scriptures and diligent, being no less than I, your nature is prone to anger; therefore, after your life ends, you shall receive an evil form."
"If I should attain the Way, I shall certainly deliver you.
Subsequently, while traveling to Guangzhou, he encountered banditry and turmoil on the road; there he met a young man.
Spitting in his hand, he drew his sword and said,
"I have truly caught you!
[The other] laughed loudly and said:
"In a past life, I owed you a debt; I have come from afar to repay it.
Your anger is merely the lingering intent from our previous existence.
Thereupon, he extended his neck to receive the blade, his countenance showing no sign of fear.
A youth killed him;
onlookers filled the streets,
all of whom were struck with wonder at this extraordinary marvel.
Subsequently, his consciousness returned to become the crown prince of the King of Anxi.
He traveled and transformed beings throughout the Central Kingdom.
During the final years of Emperor Ling’s reign, the regions of Guanzhong and Luoyang were thrown into turmoil.
Thereupon, shaking his mendicant’s staff, he traveled south to Jiangnan, saying,
"I shall pass through Mount Lu to visit my former fellow student.
Upon reaching the temple at Gongting Lake on the Yinyin River, he arrived.
This temple has long possessed divine power;
when merchants pray there, it can divide the winds to send their ships up or down the river,
so that none are delayed.
Once, there was someone who begged for his divine bamboo;
before he had granted permission, the man took it,
and the boat immediately capsized and sank.
The bamboo returned to its original place.
From then on, the boatmen were filled with reverence and awe, none of whom failed to be struck with trepidation.
Gao’s fellow travelers, numbering over thirty boats, offered sacrificial animals and prayed for blessings.
The deity then descended and instructed the invoker, saying, "There is a śramaṇa on the boat; you may call him up immediately.
All the guests were struck with amazement.
He invited Gao to enter the temple.
The deity said to Gao, "In the past,
in a foreign land, I left the household life and studied the Way together with you."
He was fond of practicing charity but was by nature prone to anger;
he is now the deity of the Yangting Temple,
governing a territory extending for a thousand li in every direction.
Because of his generosity, his treasures and playthings were exceedingly abundant;
yet because of his anger, he fell into this retribution as a spirit.
Now, seeing his former companion, his sorrow and joy are beyond description.
His life will end within days or weeks, and his hideous form will grow large;
if he should die here, he will defile the rivers and lakes,
so he must be taken across to the marshes west of the mountains.
"I fear that after this body perishes, I shall fall into hell.
I possess a thousand rolls of silk along with various precious objects;
you may use these to establish the Dharma and construct a stupa so that I may be reborn in a favorable realm."
Tao Kang said, "You have come from afar to visit me; why do you not manifest your form?
The spirit replied:
His appearance was extremely hideous and strange, such that everyone would surely have been terrified.
Baogao said, "Just go out among the crowd; they will not find it strange."
The deity emerged from behind the bed with its head;
it was a great python,
and its tail could not be seen for its length.
He approached the knees of the Exalted One;
he addressed him several times in Sanskrit and chanted several verses in praise.
The python wept with tears like rain and suddenly vanished.
Gao immediately took the silk goods, bid him farewell, and departed.
His fellow voyagers hoisted their sails.
The python then emerged from its body, climbed the mountain,
and looked out; only after the multitude raised their hands did it vanish.
In the space of a mere instant, they reached Yuzhang.
He immediately used the temple’s assets to establish Dongsi Temple.
After Gaogong departed, the deity passed away.
At dusk, a young man boarded the boat;
he knelt upright before him and received his blessing,
after which he suddenly vanished.
Gao said to the boatman,
"The youth from earlier was the deity of the Xuting Temple;
he has now been released from his evil form."
Thereupon, the temple deity ceased its activity and no longer manifested miraculous responses.
Later, people saw a dead python in a marsh to the west of the mountain.
From head to tail it spanned several *li*;
this is the present-day She Village in Xunyang Commandery.
After this, he traveled again to Guangzhou.
He sought out the youth who had harmed him in a previous life;
as the youth was still living,
he went directly to his home and recounted the matters of retribution from their past lives.
They also recounted their past karmic connections and,
facing one another with joy, said:
"We still have remaining retribution."
I shall now go to Kuaiji to see Bi Dao against the Guangzhou visitor. Wugao was extraordinary;
his mind suddenly opened to understanding, and he repented his former transgressions.
He generously provided for me with provisions as I followed Gao on my journey eastward.
He eventually reached Kuaiji.
Upon arriving, he entered the marketplace,
where it happened that a group of people were fighting in the midst of the market.
He accidentally struck the head of a tall man, who died instantly.
A traveler from Guangzhou frequently witnessed these two instances of retribution.
He then applied himself with diligence to the Buddha-dharma and recounted the circumstances in detail.
When those far and near heard of it, there was none who did not marvel at it.
[This concludes the section on] Senghui; [now for] Shi Senghui.
His secular surname was Kang;
his ancestors were people of the kingdom of Kangju,
who had lived for generations in India.
His father had moved to Jiaozhi for trade;
when he was about ten years old,
both his parents passed away.
He remained in mourning for his natural kin until the period of observance ended, whereupon he left the household life;
his conduct was exceedingly rigorous.
He was magnanimous and elegant by nature, possessing great discernment and capacity.
He was earnest in his resolve and fond of learning;
he clearly understood the Tripiṭaka and had extensively read the Six Classics.
He was extensively versed in astronomy and the *Wenzi*,
possessed a keen discernment for pivotal matters, and was quite proficient in literary composition.
At that time, Sun Quan had already established his control over the region east of the Yangtze River.
However, Buddhism had not yet spread.
In the tenth year of the Chiku era, it first reached Jianye;
there, he constructed a thatched hut, established sacred images, and practiced the Way.
At that time, the state of Wu had only recently encountered śramaṇas;
seeing their outward appearance but not yet having reached an understanding of their Way, people suspected them of practicing eccentricity for the sake of deception.
The officials reported:
"A man from the Hu tribes has entered the borders,
claiming to be a śramaṇa."
"His appearance and attire are extraordinary;
this matter should be investigated. Quan said:
Formerly, Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of a deity who called himself the Buddha.
Could that which he practiced be a remnant of his tradition?
He immediately summoned the assembly to interrogate him.
"What miraculous efficacy is there?
Hui replied,
"Since the Tathāgata passed away, more than a thousand years have suddenly elapsed."
The divine radiance of his relics and śarīra is boundless.
In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stūpas;
indeed, the establishment of stūpas and monasteries serves to manifest his enduring legacy.
Sima Quan considered this to be boastful and said to Daohui:
"If you can obtain the śarīra, I shall have a stupa built for them;
if it proves to be false, the state has established punishments."
He requested a period of seven days for the assembly and then said to his followers,
"The rise or decline of the Dharma depends upon this single undertaking."
"If we do not act with utmost sincerity now, what will avail us later? Thereupon,
they together purified themselves in a quiet chamber,
placing a copper pitcher upon a small table, burning incense, and making their reverent invocation.
When the seven-day period concluded, there was no response;
he requested an extension for another seven days,
but the result was likewise the same.
Sun Quan said, "This is a deception; I intend to punish you.
Hui further requested another twenty-one days.
Sun Quan also granted him special permission.
Dao Hui said to his fellow practitioners:
"Confucius had a saying:"
"Now that King Wen has passed away, does not the 'Cultivation' (wen) reside here?
If the Dharma-cloud were to descend in response, we would have no regrets."
"What need is there for royal punishment?
I shall simply take death as my limit.
At the end of the twenty-first day, dusk fell, yet he still saw nothing.
Everyone was struck with awe and trepidation.
Once the fifth watch had begun,
they suddenly heard a sharp metallic clang from within the jar.
He went there in person to inspect the fruit and obtained the śarīra relics.
The following morning, Quan personally held a jar in his hand and poured its contents onto a copper platter;
struck by the śarīra, the platter immediately shattered.
Wu rose in solemn awe and said,
"This is a rare and auspicious omen.
Hui then stepped forward and spoke.
The majestic spiritual power of Śāriputra is not merely manifest in his radiant physical marks;
even the fires at the end of an eon cannot burn it,
nor can the vajra-pestle shatter it.
The authorities ordered him to undergo a trial.
He then made a renewed vow, saying:
"The Dharma-cloud is about to spread its canopy; the common people look up to you for its moisture."
He prayed, "I beseech you to further manifest divine traces to extensively display your majestic spiritual power.
Thereupon, he placed the śarīra upon an iron anvil and had a strong man strike it with a hammer.
Thereupon, both the mortar and the pestle sank into the ground, yet the śarīra remained undamaged.
Sun Quan sighed in great admiration and prostration,
and immediately erected a stūpa for it.
Because this was the first Buddhist temple to be established, it was named Jianchu Monastery,
and its location was designated as Fotuo Li (Buddha Village). From this point on,
the Great Dharma flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
When Sun Hao ascended the throne, his laws and edicts were harsh and cruel; he abolished superstitious sacrifices and destroyed Buddhist temples.
Once, he ordered the imperial guards to enter the inner palace to clear the gardens, where they discovered a golden image several feet high in the ground and presented it to Hao.
Sun Hao ordered him to be placed in an impure location and doused with filthy liquid;
he and his various ministers laughed at this as a source of amusement.
In a mere instant, the man’s entire body swelled up greatly.
The private parts were especially painful,
and his cries reached the heavens.
The Grand Astrologer performed a divination and said:
Believing it was the work of a great deity,
she immediately offered prayers at various shrines to seek blessings.
The court lady then escorted the image and placed it upon the palace dais.
He washed [the image] with fragrant water dozens of times,
burned incense, and repented;
then Hao prostrated himself, knocking his head upon his pillow.
He confessed his crimes.
After a short while, when his pain had subsided,
he dispatched a messenger to the monastery to invite [the Master] to preach the Dharma.
Hui entered with him immediately.
Sun Hao questioned him in detail regarding the causes of sin and merit;
Hui analyzed and explained them for him with words that were exceedingly precise and essential.
Sima Hao possessed talent and understanding; he was greatly delighted and consequently requested to see the monastic precepts (*śramaṇa-śīla*).
However, Hui met with the fact that the text of the precepts was strictly secret and could not be lightly proclaimed.
He then took the one hundred and thirty-five vows from his original practice and divided them into two hundred and fifty matters; whether walking,
standing, sitting, or lying down, he made these vows for all sentient beings.
Upon seeing his compassionate vows so vast and universal, Shao’s benevolent mind increased all the more.
Having received the five precepts from Huihui,
his illness was cured within ten days.
He then further embellished the monastery where he resided;
throughout the imperial clan, there was none who did not revere and honor him.
During the Wu dynasty, he frequently preached the True Dharma.
Because Sun Hao was by nature fierce and coarse, he did not grasp the subtle meanings [of the teachings].
[Dao'an] therefore recounted matters of retribution and karmic response from recent times to open his mind.
In the fourth year of the Tianji era, Sun Hao surrendered to the Jin dynasty.
In the ninth month, he contracted an illness and passed away;
this was the first year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty.
Later, during the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Jin, Su Jun incited a rebellion.
The assembly hall was burned and a stupa was erected;
He Chong, the Minister of Works, further renovated and constructed it.
Zhao You, General of the Pacification of the West, did not follow the Dharma throughout his life, treating the Triple Gem with arrogance and contempt.
Upon entering this temple, he said to the various practitioners of the Way:
"This stupa has long been open and has frequently emitted radiance;
however, as it is a fabrication that contradicts the scriptures, I have been unable to believe it."
If one were to insist on seeing it for oneself, there would be nothing further to discuss.
As soon as he finished speaking, the stupa emerged, emitting five-colored light that illuminated the hall and the spire;
everyone was struck with solemn awe, their hair standing on end.
Out of this reverent faith,
another small stupa was erected to the east of the temple.
During the Yonghui era of the Tang Emperor Gaozong, the spirit appeared once again in Yue.
He was known as a wandering monk (yifang seng),
and his spirit and demeanor were so extraordinary that all who saw him were struck with awe.
Unaware of his rank,
the monastery administrators investigated the matter, rebuked him, and drove him away;
it was only when he reached the gate that they realized their error.
He then said to him, "I am Kang Senghui.
If you can preserve my true remains,"
Upon reaching the monastery,
his breath ceased as he stood for but a single step;
shortly thereafter, his eyes closed slightly.
His spirit remained unimpaired;
he raised his hand as if to receive a guest,
and his feet were poised as if about to step forward.
The assembly deliberated and lowered his sacred body to place it within the tomb;
yet, despite the exhaustion of human effort, it would not budge in the slightest.
They subsequently moved it to a superior location and erected a magnificent hall there.

The people of Yue vied with one another to offer incense, flowers, lamps, candles, silks, banners, canopies, fruits, and vessels to pray for the fulfillment of their heart's desires, which were mostly granted according to their wishes.
Initially, many of Yue’s military personnel resided at Yongxin Temple.
The women there gave birth,
and the soldiers defiled the monastic compound with pungent foods and blood;
people could no longer endure such filth and impurity.
The Master then transformed his appearance and went to visit Li Ruochu,
the Intendant of Min, saying:
"Your Excellency governs the administrative branches of Yue."
He entrusted him to serve in the military,
and having finished speaking, he brushed his robes and departed;
they subsequently searched for his traces in vain.
Lord Li was both delighted and startled;
he recorded these words, and later,
as it turned out, he did indeed go to that commandery.
Upon completing his official duties, he went to pay homage at the sacred site.
Recognizing that the person who had spoken those words at the time was this very monk,
he ordered the military household to withdraw and commanded them to take up position within their camp tents.
Furthermore, one night as a common wife was approaching her confinement, there were no lamps or candles and not even a sliver of light from the neighbors.
Suddenly, a monk entered through the window holding a candle.
When her husband arrived at Yongxin Temple the next morning, he recognized that it was Huì’s face.
This was none other than the monk who had bestowed the fire to save the woman in childbirth.
From that time on, many people among the common folk sought him out to pray for sons and daughters.
Furthermore, he once went to a commoner's house to beg for straw sandals.
To this day, many people in Yue offer *mángxié* (grass sandals) and oil-soaked banners as offerings.
Responding with miraculous efficacy, they appear before the eyes of the faithful and each visit the homes of the people.
His deeds cannot be fully recounted; he was styled Chan Master Chao-hua (Chao-hua Chanshi).
Zhu Shixing, Zhu Shixing, Zhu Shixing.
A native of Yingchuan.
Having left home to become a monk at a young age, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the scriptures.
Once, while lecturing on the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), he found the phrasing and meaning obscure;
he consequently vowed to travel afar in search of the original Sanskrit text.
Traveling westward, he reached Khotan and obtained an authentic copy of a Sanskrit manuscript.
As he was about to return to Luoyang,
the assembly of scholars from that kingdom [addressed him].
He then addressed the King, saying:
"The śramaṇas of Han wish to delude and confuse the orthodox scriptures with the books of the Brahmins.
If we do not prohibit this, I fear they will leave the land of Han deaf and blind."
The king then refused to allow the scriptures to be carried away.
Sengxing felt deep pain in his heart and consequently requested to burn the scriptures as a testament to his sincerity.
The King consented to this.
Thereupon, firewood was piled before the palace to burn him.
Facing the flames, he made a vow, saying:
"If this Great Dharma were meant to flow into the land of Han, the scriptures would not have been thus;
had there been no one to protect it, my life would have perished.
Having said this, he threw the scriptures into the fire.
The fire was immediately extinguished without damaging a single character.
The great assembly was struck with awe and submitted, all praising its divine efficacy.
Consequently, it was successfully transported to China.
Later, Shi Xing passed away in Khotan at the age of eighty.
When his body was cremated, although the firewood was exhausted and the flames extinguished, the corpse remained intact.
The assembly was all struck with wonder and astonishment.
He then uttered a spell, saying:
"If it is truly the Dharma of attaining the Way, it shall be destroyed."
At his voice, [the body] shattered and dispersed;
consequently, his bones were collected and a stūpa was erected there. Hala-kṣetra, hala-kṣetra, hala-kṣetra.
His clan and lineage are not well known.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and recited two million words of scripture.
His nature was profound and mysterious; he maintained the precepts and observed the rules of conduct. He was skilled in his deportment and possessed a handsome countenance.
He frequently practiced the dhūta austerities, dwelling alone in the mountains and wilds.
In the ninth year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he visited Luoyang briefly.
At that time, a plague was spreading, and deaths occurred in succession;
[Seng]jie performed incantations to treat them.
This was likely true in eight or nine cases out of ten.
In the first year of the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty,
he entered the west and stayed in a stone cave on Mount Luzhi, where he sat in meditation.
"This room is very far from water," he said.
At that time, people wished to open a channel for it,
but Sengjie replied:
Without requiring others' labor,
he used his own left foot to press against the stone wall to the west of the room;
the wall caved in until it reached his fingers.
Once the feet were withdrawn, water gushed forth from within;
it was fragrant, sweet, and pure, flowing without ceasing throughout the four seasons.
All who came to drink were relieved of hunger and thirst, and their illnesses were cured.
In the eighth year of the Yuan Kang era, he sat upright and passed away.
His disciples cremated him according to the laws of the land;
the burning continued for several days.
Yet the corpse remained seated within the fire, never turning to ash.
It was then moved back into the stone chamber.
"Jīvaka, Jīvaka, Jīvaka. [End of section]
He was a man from India who traveled extensively among the Chinese and the barbarians, having no fixed abode;
he was unconventional and possessed of extraordinary spiritual powers.
He was unrestrained and suddenly abandoned worldly traces, his conduct being inconsistent;
people of the time could not fathom him.
From his departure from India until his arrival in Funan, [his path remained obscure].
Having traveled along the various seacoasts and ventured as far as Jiaozhi and Guangzhou,
he encountered many miraculous and extraordinary occurrences.
Upon reaching Xiangyang, he arrived at his destination.
He wished to be carried across the river,
but the boatman, seeing that the Brahmin śramaṇa’s robes were tattered and worn,
treated him with disdain and would not take him aboard.
When the boat reached the northern bank, he had already crossed over and was proceeding forward.
He saw two tigers;
the tigers lowered their ears and wagged their tails.
Fayou stroked its head with his hand,
and the tiger descended the path and departed.
Those who witnessed this on both banks followed after it in great crowds.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, [Seng]yu arrived in Luoyang.
When everyone there prostrated themselves to pay their respects,
Yu remained kneeling in the Hu fashion, his countenance and expression remaining entirely composed and unmoving.
At times, he would inform others of his previous incarnations,
stating that Zhi Fayuan had come from among sheep,
while Zhu Fayu had come from among humans.
Furthermore, he criticized the various members of the Sangha, saying that their robes were too magnificent and did not accord with the simple dharma.
Upon seeing the palace city of Luoyang, he remarked,
"It resembles the celestial palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
It is simply that natural phenomena and human affairs differ from one another.
Daoyu said to the śramaṇa Jīśāmī:
"The craftsman who built this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Once it was completed, he returned to the heavens.
Beneath the roof tiles of the house, there should be fifteen hundred crafted vessels.
At that time, everyone said, "We have heard in the past that this craftsman indeed placed crafted vessels beneath the tiles."
At that time, Teng Yongwen of Nanyang, the Governor of Hengyang,
was residing at Manshui Temple in Luoyang;
both his legs were cramped and bent, rendering him unable to rise or walk.
Zhiyu went to see him and said,
"If you wish for your illness to be cured,
why not fetch a cup of pure water and a branch of willow?"
Daoyi then brushed the water with a willow branch and raised his hand toward Yongwen, reciting a mantra;
he did this three times.
He then pressed down on Yongwen’s knee with his hand to make him stand up.
Immediately he rose and walked as before.
In this monastery, there were several dozen withered *cintāmaṇi* trees (wish-fulfilling trees).
Daoyu asked Yongwen:
"How long has the tree been dead?
Yongwen replied,
"It has been for many years."
Fayou then recited a spell over the tree according to the "Method for Reciting the Yongwen" (Yongwen fa).
Immediately, the tree sprouted new shoots and flourished with luxuriant foliage.
At that time, during the height of summer, there was a man suffering from a malignant tumor who was on the verge of death.
He placed a bowl upon the patient's abdomen,
covered it entirely with a white cloth,
and recited thousands of words of incantation and aspiration.
Immediately, a foul odor permeated the entire room.
The patient said, "I am alive."
Fayou ordered someone to lift the cloth,
and inside the alms bowl there were several liters of what appeared to be mud;

Every morning they would gather there;
dogs and rats ate together until the courtyard was filled with their droppings,
as both monastics and laypeople watched them.
At one time, he lost a mouse.
He was deeply grieved and despondent, thinking,
"This must have been killed by the dog."
He then rebuked the dog, and the dog immediately bit it and brought it back.
Seeing this, Shen Qin was distressed and struck the dog with his staff.
Having buried the mouse, he wept with bitter grief.
The monks, whose robes and chests had been gnawed by the mice, informed Cen of this.
Cen summoned all the mice and ordered them to look after one another.
A rat had no protector.
Cen said, "Why did you bite my clothes? and he struck it with a staff.
The rats did not dare to move.
Because the temple was poor, Cen established a kitchen and storehouse at the White Horse Spring (Baima Quan) beneath the lecture hall, near the Luo pond, as recorded in the *Yanji*.
He designated a certain location for the kitchen and storehouse.
He designated a certain place as a granary,
and everyone laughed at him.
After one night had passed, the water receded and the land emerged exactly as he had said.
He then acted accordingly, causing [the offerings] to become abundant.
Furthermore, he recorded in a distant prophecy:
"Sixty years hence, there shall be a foolish man who will erect a multi-storied pavilion to the south of this temple."
However, although the temple’s foundations and assets were not diminished, it was impossible to reside there due to litigation.
During the Yonghui era, someone happened to erect a multi-storied pavilion;
consequently, they engaged in legal disputes exactly as had been foretold.
Huiwu, Huiwu, Shi Huiwu. His clan and lineage are unknown.
He lived in seclusion among the Taibai Mountains, where he recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
While he was taking pine and horsetail as medicinal tonics,
he suddenly saw a lay practitioner at one point who came and said,
"I invite you. The lay practitioner then leaped into the air.
He caused [the practitioner] to awaken while seated within his sash;
gathering him up, they flew through the air to a certain place of practice,
where he saw five hundred heterodox monks arriving, soaring through the sky.
Wu suddenly passed away while engaged in his final practices.
The layman said to him,
"Master, you have upheld the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which is the realm of the Buddhas."
"How can you take a seat below that of a Lesser Sage?
He then led [the monk] to a position above five hundred people.
When the meal was finished, the lay devotee said:
"The intention behind the vegetarian feast at our monastery was solely for the sake of the Master.
Although five hundred arhats came to partake, they were all invited only at the last moment.
He then sent him back to his original location.
It was as if waking from a dream.
This occurred during the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong. Regarding the Dharma Master Fa’rong:
[the text] "Fa’rong" is the name of the Dharma Master Fa’rong.
His surname was Wei.
A native of Yanling in Runzhou,
he entered Mount Mao at the age of nineteen to rely upon Dharma Master Jing, where he shaved his head, served him with diligence, and sought the Way.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era, he established a thatched meditation hut on the northern cliff below Youqi Temple at Mount Niutou.
Day and night, he engaged in contemplation and discernment, never missing a single moment of time.
On the mountain was a stone chamber, deep for about ten paces.
Daorong sat within it when suddenly a divine serpent appeared, over ten feet long.
His eyes were like sparks of fire as he raised his head and displayed a majestic air.
He stayed overnight at the entrance of the chamber;
seeing that Huirong remained motionless, he finally departed.
He resided there for one hundred days.
The mountain was naturally infested with tigers,
such that even those who gathered firewood were absent.
After she had merged with them, her coming and going was unimpeded.
Furthermore, she felt that a herd of deer relied upon her chamber to listen for her voice and remained crouched there, never showing any sign of fear;
even two large deer would enter directly.
He stayed for three years to listen to the Dharma with the community of monks before departing.
The site of his residence and dining kitchen bordered a large stream;
since the water surged there, it was impossible to construct steps.
He then looked back and paced about, pointing toward the eastern ridge and saying,
"In the past, Master Huiyuan leaned his staff against this weathered rock and was startled by the spring;
it would be fitting to dwell here."
It was destined that a clear spring would overflow from within.
Overnight, a flying spring suddenly gushed forth on the eastern ridge;
its water was pure, white, sweet, and delicious—warm in winter and cold in summer.
He immediately urged [the master] to ascend the peak and proceed toward the cauldron via the corridor.
Furthermore, in the eleventh month of the twenty-first year,
he lectured on the Lotus Sūtra beneath the cliff.
At that time, while fresh snow filled the steps and the flow of the Dharma remained uninterrupted,
two stalks of flowers were found within the frozen ice;
they resembled lotuses and were as brilliant as gold.
After seven days, he suddenly lost it.
In the third year of the Yonghui era, the magistrate of the district requested him to come forth and lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at Jianchu Monastery;
a congregation of one thousand monks gathered, and they reached the "Chapter on the Cessation of Disputes."
Rong then unleashed his natural eloquence to deliberate upon the principles and meanings;
suddenly the earth shook violently, startling his companions with its waves,
while the bells, chimes, and incense stands all swayed and trembled.
Those inside and outside the temple, both monastics and laypeople, remained peaceful and unaware.
In the first year of the Xianqing era (656), Xiao Yuanshan, the Director of the Office of Merit, invited him repeatedly;
he then departed for Jianchu Monastery.
Tao Rong said to the monks,
"From now on, once we depart, there will be no expectation of meeting again.
This is the constant rule regarding the way of parting and reuniting."
He declined the offer but could not avoid it;
he subsequently departed from the mountain gate.
The birds and beasts wailed in mourning for over a month without ceasing.
The mountain streams, springs, and ponds struck by stones overflowed with sand, filling them all at once.
The four large paulownia trees in front of the hall, which had been lush and flourishing in the fifth month,
withered away overnight.
In the second year [of the reign], on the twenty-third day of the intercalary first month, he passed away at Jianchu.
He was sixty-four years of age.
Zhiqin—Zhiqin is the monk Zhiqin.
His secular surname was Zhu.
During the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, Daxingguo Monastery was established separately in Sheli Prefecture.
Since his youth, Qin had made it his life's purpose to protect and uphold the Dharma.
Whenever he spoke among the assembly, his words were invariably harmonious and conciliatory.
Through his refined sincerity and courageous diligence, all matters received divine protection from the unseen realm.
Initially, when his mother fell ill and was severely prostrate, he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara for her sake.
Upon the leaves of the trees within the residence, transformation Buddhas appeared;
the entire family saw them together,
and the mother’s illness was subsequently cured.
Furthermore, during the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, when various bandits rose up in competition,
Daqin alone guarded this temple so that the bandits did not dare to assault it;
thus, the temple buildings, scriptures, and statues remained entirely undamaged.
The various monasteries had fallen into ruin and could no longer be seen with the eye.
On another occasion, he temporarily donned secular clothing to avoid the blades of weapons;
surrounded by bandits who intended to kill him, he remained there.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air announcing:
"Master, you may discard your secular clothes.
Thereupon, he removed his outer garments.
The bandits saw him, prostrated in worship,
and invited him to accept their offerings.
This continued for several months.
Later, he went to Shu to listen to Dharma Master Gao lecture;
the assembly numbered three thousand,
and the Master entrusted him with the supervision of all matters.
Consequently, he attained peace and stability, and there were no disturbances within or without; this was due to the power of a single individual.
Later, during the early Tang dynasty, he returned to Dengzhou, where he lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Tri-svabhāva-śāstra* more than ten times.
Later, he went into seclusion on the Northern Mountain, remaining there for over ten years.
The three locations where he resided still exist today.
He constantly heard the sound of bells within the valley.
Later, while searching among the rocky peaks, he suddenly beheld a temple;
it was exquisitely beautiful and extraordinary beyond the ordinary.
He entered within and paid his respects.
It was as if someone were dwelling there.
After searching several times in this manner,
he could no longer find where they were located.
Furthermore, while he was staying in the mountains, his provisions were nearly exhausted.
At the places where he practiced his path, the earth spontaneously rose up;
he cleared it away, yet on the following day it did so again.
This happened two or three times in succession,
until grain finally appeared.
Thereupon, he dug deeply and obtained more than twenty *shí* of millet.
The grains were as large as millet seeds and reddish in color, slightly different from ordinary cereals.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma was declining in Dengzhou;
the monastics and laypeople of Hezhou went to the mountain to pay their respects and make an invitation.
He wished to emerge as the abbot,
and consequently emerged following a dream;
however, the details of that dream were not clearly recorded.
Later, as he was carrying the image out of the mountain, it suddenly grew dark midway; unable to discern the path, he could not proceed.
Suddenly, two extraordinary torches appeared, illuminating the road with brilliant light.
Because he had attained the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), he was escorted back to the village;
only then did the fire subside, and all the villagers witnessed this without fail, being struck with wonder and amazement.
At the beginning of the Yonghui era, because the affairs of the world were complex and distracting, he remained in his room and did not go out.
Having studied for nearly three years, he read all the sutras twice.
Every time he was reading a sutra, he constantly saw spirits come to listen.
During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he frequently heard the sounds of finger-snapping and clearing one's throat.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Xianqing era,
prior to his passing, he devoted himself day and night to completing all meritorious works that had been incomplete.
When someone asked why he was so suddenly in such haste,
he replied,
"How can the law of impermanence be relied upon?"
On the fifteenth day,
the branches and leaves of the trees within the monastery withered and fell away of their own accord,
and the birds cried out in lamentation throughout the monastery grounds.
The monks were each startled and questioned one another, not knowing the cause.
When the morning of the sixteenth day arrived, they suddenly saw the spirit who had previously listened to the sutras coming to prostrate;
he spoke, saying, "Do not prostrate."
No bystanders saw him; he then shaved his head,
donned his robes, and sat cross-legged within the corded couch, holding a censer in his hand.
He addressed his disciples:
"You should take up the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra and recite it until you reach the end of the 'Chapter on Rebirth'."
He then sat with palms joined and passed away.
After he had been laid out for several days, his complexion remained as it was before.
A constant, extraordinary fragrance was wafted throughout the temple.
He was seventy-four years old.
Regarding Daoxuan: Daoxuan, whose secular surname was Qian, was a monk of the Shi school.
He was a native of Dantu.
Initially, while his mother was pregnant, she dreamed that the moon pierced her womb;
she further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to her:
"The child you are carrying is none other than Sengyou, the Vinaya Master of the Liang dynasty.
Sengyou was formerly the monk Senghu of Yingue Temple on Mount Shanxi during the Southern Qi dynasty;
it is fitting that he follow the path of renunciation."
Having reached the age of twenty, he exerted himself to protect and uphold the Dharma with single-minded devotion and self-restraint.
Moved by his sincerity, śarīra relics manifested within his precious casket;
thereupon, he withdrew from public view to dwell in the valley of Zhangzhang on Mount Zhongnan.
A water spirit pointed out the location where he resided;
after digging more than one chi into the ground, a spring gushed forth.
At that time, it was called Baekchon-sa (White Spring Temple).
Fierce beasts were tamed and submissive, each finding its refuge there;
famous flowers were fragrant and wondrous grasses spread far and wide.
At the end of the Sui dynasty, he moved to Fengde Temple.
Once, while sitting in solitude,
a Dharma-protecting deity informed him:
"That village of Qingguan was formerly the Jingye Monastery."
The ground shall possess the power of jewels, and the Way may be practiced and perfected.
Hearing this, one takes it as a sign:
burning the incense of merit and practicing the boat of Prajñā through meditative concentration.
At that time, a group of nāgas came to pay their respects;
whether male or female, they transformed themselves into human forms.
The śrāmaṇera, with a distracted mind, looked about and gazed at them with a sidelong glance.
The dragon became incensed and was about to seize and devour him; however,
he immediately repented and spat his venom into the well,
explaining everything in detail before departing.
Xuan then ordered it to be sealed shut;
yet people sometimes secretly opened it, and smoke would often rise from within.
Observing these divine transformations, he once sent a casket containing extraordinary flowers.
Its shape resembles that of a jujube flower, and its size is like that of a jujube seed.
Its fragrance is exquisite and pervasive; even after several years, it remains perfectly intact.
Furthermore, he offered rare fruits such as plums, apricots, pears, and crabapples.
Its flavor was sweet and its color pure, unlike anything encountered in the human world.
His disciples once wished to report a private matter;
however, this had already been secretly communicated beforehand.
Using meditative concentration to observe the faculties and administer medicine according to the ailment—
all cases are of this kind.
Xuan once constructed an altar.
Suddenly, there appeared a monk with long eyebrows who spoke of knowing the Way;
furthermore, a Brahmin monk of the third fruit stage prostrated at the altar and praised it, saying:
Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you alone have been the one to cause the Semblance Dharma to flourish and arise while it remains in the world.
In the spring of the second year of the Qiánfēng era, he was mysteriously moved by a celestial being who came to discourse with him on the characteristics of the Vinaya.

Regarding the errors found within the *Chao-wen qingzhong yi* (The Ritual of the Light and Heavy Codes of the Transcribed Text), these are all the fault of the translator and not the crime of the Master.
I request that the Master correct them;
therefore, most of the works currently in circulation are revised versions of his original texts.
Furthermore, there was a celestial being who once compiled the *Ji-huan tu-jing* (Illustrated Scripture of Jetavana);
it is said to consist of approximately one hundred scrolls of paper and silk from the human realm.
During the Zhenguan era, he once lived in seclusion at Yunshishan in Qinfu.

People saw a celestial youth attending to him on his left and right. At Ximing Monastery, while performing the night walking meditation (caṅkrama), as his feet were about to step onto the front steps, something supported them so that he walked through the air without harm.
Looking at him closely, he realized it was a youth.
Xuān immediately asked who he was to be there in the middle of the night.
The youth replied:
"I am no ordinary person; I am Nanda, the son of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, I have guarded the Upādhyāya for a long time."
Xuanchi said, "This poor monk practices the Way without concern; there is no need to trouble the Crown Prince.
Your Majesty’s majestic power is sovereign and free."
"In the Western Regions there are things that can be used for Buddhist services;
I pray you will procure them for me.
The Prince said:
I have long possessed this precious Buddha-tooth relic in my hand; though it is as dear as my own head or eyes, I dare not fail to offer it.
Shortly thereafter, he bestowed it upon Xuān.
Xuān Bǎojiū made offerings to him.
Furthermore, one day a celestial being came to the courtyard to pay his respects and said to Xuān:
The Vinaya Master was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, where he held a bundle of items and said,
"This is the 'thorny forest incense' (kaṇṭaka-vana-gandha).
Thereafter, he sat in meditation for ten weeks and passed away.
It was the third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Qianfeng era.
He was seventy-two years of age and had fifty-two years of monastic seniority.
Master Yingshi, the Zen Master Ying,
resided at Fahai Temple in the Western Capital.
A strange person came to visit him and said:
The disciple knows that there exists the Water and Land Feast (shuilu zhai), which can benefit both the hidden realm and the world of light.
Since the passing of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, however, it has been neglected and no longer practiced.
Now, at Dajue Monastery, the Wu monk Yijie preserves the ritual texts for this ceremony.
I pray that you, Master, will go and seek [the necessary items].
On the fifteenth day of the coming month, at the temple north of the mountain, perform the ritual according to the Dharma.
If I am indeed released from this prison, I shall not dare to fail to repay your kindness.
The Duke then went to Yijie, obtained the ritual texts, and returned home; he immediately prepared the offerings at Shanbei Temple on the appointed day.
At dusk the following day, the aforementioned extraordinary person arrived with a dozen or so companions to express their gratitude, saying:
"The disciple was none other than the Qin King Zhuangxiang.
He then pointed to his followers and said,
"These are Fan Sui, Ranghou, Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Zhang Yi, and Chen Zhen."
They were all subjects of Qin.
All sat in confinement within the dark realm of the underworld for their original crimes;
in the profound darkness of the great night, none could provide rescue or protection.
Formerly, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty established this vegetarian feast at Jinshan Temple,
the subjects of King Zhou from previous dynasties were all relieved of their sufferings;
at that time, my disciples also temporarily ceased their suffering.
However, as the details of the legal case have not yet been resolved, we have been unable to escape. Now,
having received the invitation for this vegetarian feast provided by our Master,
we, your disciples along with these companions, [are here].

The various lords and nobles of the neighboring states, all riding upon the power of their wholesome roots and about to be born into the human realm, feared that the world was changing and the nations were becoming distinct; therefore, they came to offer their thanks.
Having finished speaking, they suddenly vanished.
From then on, these ritual texts were disseminated throughout the world, bringing great benefit.
Kuiji— Kuiji, the commentator Kuiji—
whose courtesy name was Hongdao.
His surname was Wei-chi,
and he was a native of Chang’an in Jingzhao.
Initially, his birth mother was Lady Pei.
In a dream, she swallowed a lunar disc with her palm;
upon waking, she became pregnant.
When the months were full, [the child was born].
He was unlike other children of his age;
as he repeatedly recited and studied [the scriptures], his mind became spiritually enlightened and his spirit refined.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he entered the monastic community.
Upon entering the Dharma, he was appointed by imperial decree as a disciple of Xuanzang and initially resided at Guangfu Temple.
Shortly thereafter, he was selected by imperial decree from among those who were exceptionally intelligent and outstanding.
He entered the Great Ci'en Monastery to personally serve Master Xuanzang and study the various Buddha-dharmas.
Later, he traveled to Mount Wutai and ascended Mount Taihang,
eventually staying overnight in an ancient Buddhist temple in the West River region.
In a dream, he saw himself at the base of a mountain cliff where countless people were crying out in agony;
amidst the darkness, he could hardly bear to hear it.
He then ascended those layered peaks on foot.
All were the color of lapis lazuli;
they saw all the lands and looked up toward a single city.
Within that city, a voice spoke, saying:
"Stop, stop! Ho!
Master Ki ought not to have come this far.
At that moment, two divine youths emerged from the city.
Question: "Do you see the sentient beings suffering from their offenses beneath the mountain?
Answer: "I do."
"I have heard your voice but do not see your form.
The youth then handed him a sword, saying,
"If you cut open your belly, you shall see."
Jizang cut open his own belly;
as it opened, two streams of light shone forth, illuminating the foot of the mountain,
where he saw countless people undergoing suffering.
At that time, the youth entered the city carrying two sheets of paper and a brush, which he offered up and departed.
Daokiji was utterly amazed and astonished.
The next day, he obtained the *Maitreya-sūtra on Rebirth Above* within the monastery.
Considering him to be a manifestation of Maitreya,
and wishing to expand upon [the teachings],
he then took up his brush and bestowed [the instructions].
Śarīra relics fell in succession from the tip of his brush.
He once fashioned an image of Mañjuśrī out of jade and transcribed the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in gold;
in both instances, he obtained auspicious responses.
Initially, Master Daoxuan, through his propagation of the Vinaya, moved the heavenly kitchen to provide him with offerings of food.
Daoyi, however, always held the "Three Vehicles" in low esteem and did not regard them as objects of ritual veneration.
Daoyi once visited Daoxuan.
The day passed noon,
yet the celestial meal did not arrive;
it was only when Daokai took his leave that the deity descended.
After he had finished his reprimand,
a celestial deity said,
"I have just seen a Mahāyāna bodhisattva here."
The guards were extremely strict;
thus, he could not enter on his own.
When Xuán heard of this, he was greatly alarmed.
Consequently, those both far and near increased their reverence for him.
Previously, Master Xuanzang had personally sought out the masters Śīlabhadra and Asaṅga in the Western Regions to study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the Vijñaptimātra school;
the Master [Śikṣānanda] fully grasped all their subtle essentials.
The world calls this the Cien Teaching.
He passed away on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Yongchun era at the Sutra Translation Hall of Ci'en Monastery.
He was fifty-one years of age.
Hongbang (洪昉). Shi Hongbang was originally a native of Jingzhao.
Having entered the monastic order in his youth, he subsequently realized the fruits of the Path.
His aspiration was set upon meditative stillness, yet he also took the lecturing of sutras as his primary task.
His disciples constantly numbered in the hundreds.
One day, at the beginning of the night, Fang sat alone.
Four men came forward and said, "The King of Ghosts, Yama, has now prepared a vegetarian feast for the sake of his younger daughter’s illness; we request that you, Master, deign to attend.
Baofang said:
"We are humans; you are ghosts.
How were you able to come here?
The four replied:
"Master, you simply proceed;
I, your disciple, shall be able to bring it about.
Fang followed his advice.
Four men mounted horses,
each carrying one leg of a rope bed, and proceeded northward for several hundred li.
They arrived at a mountain,
where there was again a small vermilion gate;
the four men requested that Fang close his eyes.
Before he had even finished his meal,
someone said,
"He has already arrived at the royal court."
The palaces and chambers were exceptionally lofty and grand;
the attendants were solemnly adorned, much like those of a sovereign.
The King of Ghosts, wearing his crown and robes, descended the steps to receive him with formal courtesy.
The king said,
"I have a young daughter who has long been ill;
she is now fortunately recovered."
I wish to cultivate a small amount of merit by observing a single fast;
for this reason, I have invited you, Master, to attend.
Once the fast is concluded, I shall personally escort you back, so you need have no concern.
Thereupon, he was invited into the palace.
The site of the purification ritual was magnificently adorned and splendid;
there were nearly ten thousand monks and an immense number of Buddha images.
It was just like human affairs:
looking up into the sky, one could not see the bright sun, appearing as if there were a heavy,
oppressive gloom like that of the human world.
In a short while, the king’s consort and several hundred ladies of the inner court all came forth to pay their respects.
Among them was the king’s daughter, aged fourteen or fifteen,
whose appearance alone bore the pallor of illness.
Fang began serving as the ritual assistant.
When the vow was completed, he saw several people carrying more than a thousand ivory trays with food arrive;
they were placed in order before the seated monks.
On the great bed, exquisite food had been specially prepared, which was exceedingly fragrant and pure.
As Fang was about to eat it,
the King of Ghosts said to him:
"If the Master remains here for long, you shall have to consume the food of ghosts.
We dare not detain you;
we pray that you do not eat."
Fang was struck with fear and stopped.
When the fast-breaking meal was finished,
several hundred plates of leftover food still remained.
When [Wang] Fang first saw that his attendants and officials, numbering nearly a thousand, all had the look of those wishing to eat,
he requested that the King grant them the remains of the food.
The King said:
He hurriedly took it and presented it to him.
The officials bowed in thanks, looking at one another with joyful smiles;
their mouths were so wide open that they reached both ears.
The King then knelt and said,
"Since you have graced me with your presence, Master, I have no other offering to provide;
I offer five hundred bolts of silk to you."
"Please receive for me the Eightfold Precepts of the Fasting Retreat.
The Master said,
"It is paper made of ghost-silk."
"I do not need it.
The King said,
"There is someone else who offers silk to the Master."
Because he had observed the eightfold precepts of the fast, once the observance was concluded,
the king again ordered the previous four men to escort him back as before.
Bao-fang suddenly opened his eyes and found himself already at his residence;
it was still not yet dawn.
His disciples merely thought that he had entered meditative absorption and was unaware of where he had gone.
Fang suddenly opened his eyes and ordered a lamp to be lit to illuminate the bed;
there, the five hundred bolts of silk were found.
His disciples questioned him about this.
He then explained the reason for this.
Since Bao-fang had long been renowned for his excellence in dhyāna practice, his reputation was flourishing daily;
recently, when he arrived at the place of the ghost, it was merely his spirit that went there.
Yet his form remained motionless.
Before long, while he was sitting at dawn,
there were two celestial beings whose physical forms were exceptionally beautiful.
He paid his respects and requested, saying,
"The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra invites the Master to come to the heavens for offerings.
Baofang granted his permission.
Because he had spread out a celestial robe for Fang to sit upon,
the two men grasped the robe and ascended into the air;
in a mere moment, they arrived in the Southern Heaven.
The King, leading his attendants, bowed deeply and paid homage, saying:
"Your Reverence’s practice of the Way is lofty and far-reaching;
the various devas wish to behold Your Reverence as you preach and recite."
For this reason, he immediately requested that Master [Seng]fang be invited;
accordingly, a high seat was prepared for him to sit upon.
His place of practice (dōjō) was so magnificent and beautiful that it surpassed anything in the human world by more than a hundred thousandfold.
The devas and humans were all tall and possessed bodies of radiant light.
Their palaces and trees were all made of the seven treasures, all of which emitted such brilliance that they dazzled the eyes of men.
When Fang first arrived in heaven, his physical form was still like that of a human.
He saw that after the Heavenly King’s body had grown large to equal that of the devas,
various precious delicacies appeared spontaneously,
possessing an extraordinary sweetness and flavor.
When the meal was finished, the King invited him into the palace,
where he provided further offerings and engaged him in cordial conversation.
His retinue consisted of a great multitude of celestial officials as well as spirits and deities.
Later, he suddenly said,
"I, your disciple, wish to go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to deliberate on certain matters;
I request that you, Master, remain here for a short while."
He further instructed his attendants, saying,
"The Master wishes to travel and visit various places; you may permit him to do so,
but do not allow him to go to the rear garden."
Having spoken thus repeatedly, he departed.
After he had gone, Fang thought to himself, "What harm could there be in the rear garden that he does not wish me to go there?
Taking advantage of a moment when no one was about, he secretly went to the rear garden.
The garden was exceedingly vast, with flowing springs, ponds, and marshes;
trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs were found everywhere.
As one gradually delved deeper, these were not things recognized in the human world.
From afar, he heard the sound of great groans and shrieks, unbearable to hear.

He then went to their side and saw a massive bronze pillar, several hundred feet in diameter and a thousand *zhang* in height; the pillar had perforations that reached through from one side to the other.
Some had their heads bound with silver chains,
while others had their breastbones pierced;
such instances numbered in the tens of thousands.
Their heads were all those of yakṣas;
with saw-like teeth and hook-shaped claws, their bodies were twice the size of devas.
